You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

" * Returns an exact representation of the Binomial * Coefficient, "n choose k", the number of * k-element subsets that can be selected from an * n-element set. *

* Preconditions: *

    *
  • 0 <= k <= n (otherwise * IllegalArgumentException is thrown)
    • *
  • The result is small enough to fit into a long. The * largest value of n for which all coefficients are * < Long.MAX_VALUE is 66. If the computed value exceeds * Long.MAX_VALUE an ArithMeticException is * thrown.
    • *

* * @param n the size of the set * @param k the size of the subsets to be counted * @return n choose k * @throws IllegalArgumentException if preconditions are not met. * @throws ArithmeticException if the result is too large to be represented * by a long integer. "

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test iterates over all n ≤ 200 and k ≤ n and compares MathUtils.binomialCoefficient(n, k) against an exact, overflow-checked recursive implementation used within the test helper (MathUtilsTest.binomialCoefficient). For n ≤ 66, it expects no exceptions and exact equality of results; for n > 66, it allows ArithmeticException when overflow occurs, but still compares behaviors and values when both compute a result.

Inspecting MathUtils.binomialCoefficient(int, int) shows the problem:
- After trivial cases (k = 0, 1, n, n − 1), it computes
  long result = Math.round(binomialCoefficientDouble(n, k)); (line 184)
  and then returns result (line 208).
- All the comments that follow (about symmetry, exact multiplicative computation with gcd factoring, and overflow-safe steps) are not implemented; the method returns immediately with the double-based approximation.

binomialCoefficientDouble(int, int) itself is:
- return Math.floor(Math.exp(binomialCoefficientLog(n, k)) + 0.5); (line 236)

binomialCoefficientLog(int, int) computes:
- Sum of logs of factorial ratios using double precision (lines 286–298).

This design makes binomialCoefficient rely entirely on floating-point log/exp and a nearest-integer rounding to return a long. For large coefficients near the long range limit (but still within range for n ≤ 66), double precision cannot represent the exact integer values (double has 53-bit precision, ~16 decimal digits), and the accumulated roundoff from summing logs and exponentiation can exceed ±0.5 in the unit space at those magnitudes. As a result, the nearest-integer rounding can yield an off-by-one (or more) error, violating exactness.

This directly explains:
- The test’s equality assertion failing for large in-range values, e.g., the reported identity C(65,32) + C(65,33) = C(66,33) fails because at least one of these values is misrounded by the double-based computation.
- The third assertion (that there should be no exception for n ≤ 66) is still typically satisfied because exp(log) for these n does not overflow to infinity, so Math.round does not saturate to Long.MAX_VALUE; however, the returned value is wrong due to rounding error, causing the equality checks to fail.

In short, MathUtils.binomialCoefficient(int, int) is incorrectly implemented: it returns a rounded double approximation instead of an exact integer computed via a safe multiplicative algorithm. The code even contains comments outlining the intended exact approach (using symmetry, gcd-based factor splitting, and careful overflow checks for n ≤ 66), but that logic is missing. This is the root cause of the failures in testBinomialCoefficientLarge and the reported identity checks near Long.MAX_VALUE.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).

MathUtils.binomialCoefficient(int, int)
MathUtils.binomialCoefficientDouble(int, int)
MathUtils.binomialCoefficientLog(int, int)
